ACCELERATING SECURITY ALERT HANDLING WITH ARCTIC WOLF AURORA AGENTIC SOC Hello everyone! Today, I’d like to share an intriguing solution from AWS and Arctic Wolf that leverages AI agents within the cybersecurity domain. The “Aurora Agentic SOC” solution helps organizations process security alerts more efficiently by combining artificial intelligence with a team of security experts.
3.1.1 The Challenge
During system operations, organizations frequently receive a high volume of security alerts from tools such as Amazon GuardDuty and AWS Security Hub. Often, security teams lack the time and personnel required to thoroughly investigate and analyze every single alert.
This can lead to delays in detecting and addressing threats, thereby increasing the risk to system security.
3.1.2 The Arctic Wolf Solution
Figure 3.1: Architecture of Arctic Wolf Aurora Agentic SOC on AWS.
Arctic Wolf has developed the Aurora Agentic SOC, which utilizes AI agents in tandem with security experts to automate the alert-handling process.
The system operates through the following workflow:
Alert Collection: AWS Security Hub aggregates findings from various security services.
Data Transmission: Amazon EventBridge detects new events, Amazon Data Firehose forwards the data, and AWS Lambda processes and enriches it with additional information.
Analysis: AI agents on the Aurora platform assist in categorizing alerts, conducting investigations, and determining the level of risk.
Resolution: Security experts review complex cases and collaborate to implement appropriate response measures. 3.1.3 Why is this approach effective?
The key strength of this solution lies in the synergy between AI and human expertise. AI agents handle repetitive tasks, analyze large volumes of alerts, and support continuous investigation, while security experts focus on complex scenarios that require in-depth assessment.
Furthermore, an event-driven architecture ensures that alerts are routed to the processing system the moment they occur, eliminating the need for continuous, periodic data polling.
3.1.4 Achieved Results According to an AWS article, when CloudHesive implemented Arctic Wolf, the following results were observed:
A 50% reduction in the number of alerts requiring initial analysis.
A 99% increase in the speed of investigation and remediation.
A 10-fold cost saving compared to the estimated expense of building an in-house Security Operations Center (SOC).
These outcomes demonstrate the potential of combining AI agents with human experts in cybersecurity operations. 3.1.5 Personal Reflections & Conclusion
In my view, this article offers a practical perspective on applying AI within the field of security. AI goes beyond simply answering questions; it can also actively participate in analysis, investigation, and the coordinated response to security incidents.
Through this piece, I have gained a better understanding of the roles that AWS services—such as Security Hub, EventBridge, Lambda, and S3—play in building automated security monitoring systems. This knowledge is also highly valuable for deepening my grasp of cloud computing architecture and the trends surrounding the adoption of AI in enterprise environments.
Author: Kieu Minh Quang
References: AWS – Resolve Security Signals Faster with Arctic Wolf’s Aurora Agentic SOC

BLOG 2: BUILDING A METERING SYSTEM FOR SAAS ON AWS ​​MARKETPLACE USING METERING AGENT SKILL Leveraging AI Agents and AWS Serverless to Automate SaaS Usage Tracking Hello everyone! Today, I’d like to share an intriguing AWS solution that utilizes AI Agents in the development of SaaS systems. The “AWS Marketplace Metering Agent Skill” helps developers build, deploy, and test systems for tracking service usage, thereby enabling more accurate customer billing.
3.2.1 The Challenge For SaaS products listed on AWS Marketplace, businesses need to track the volume of resources or services consumed by customers in order to implement usage-based billing.
However, building a custom metering system from scratch involves handling numerous complexities—such as customer registration, usage data collection, data aggregation, and the submission of billing information—which makes the development process both complicated and time-consuming.
3.2.2 The AWS Solution Figure 3.2: Architecture of the SaaS usage metering system on AWS Marketplace.
AWS has introduced the “Metering Agent Skill,” a tool designed to assist AI agents in building SaaS metering systems directly within an AI-integrated development environment.
The solution operates through several key components:
AI Agent and AWS MCP Server: Facilitate the retrieval of guidance, analysis of requirements, and generation of integration code. AWS SAM and CloudFormation: Automate the creation and deployment of necessary AWS resources. Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda: Handle customer registration information and process data. Amazon EventBridge and Amazon SQS: Manage event orchestration, scheduling, and the transmission of usage data. Amazon DynamoDB: Store customer information, licenses, and usage data. BatchMeterUsage API: Submit usage data in batches to AWS Marketplace for billing purposes. 3.2.3 Why is this approach effective? A standout feature of this solution is the use of an AI agent to automate various stages of system development. Instead of manually writing all the source code and configuring each individual AWS service, developers can simply describe their requirements, and the agent will assist in generating the necessary code and deployment templates.
Furthermore, the system supports a “dry-run” testing mode, allowing for the verification of workflows without actually submitting live billing data. This helps mitigate risks before the system goes into production.
3.2.4 Implementation considerations To utilize the Metering Agent Skill, developers must have an AWS Marketplace Seller account and a SaaS product configured with a usage-based billing model.
Additionally, any source code generated by the AI ​​should be reviewed for security and compliance before being deployed in a production environment. Enterprises also need to implement the logic for recording SaaS application usage data into DynamoDB themselves, as this component is not automatically deployed by the Agent.
3.2.5 Personal Assessment & Conclusion In my view, this is a valuable solution for businesses developing SaaS products on AWS Marketplace. Combining an AI Agent with serverless services simplifies the process of building a metering system and reduces the need for manual configuration.
Through this article, I have gained a better understanding of how to integrate Amazon EventBridge, AWS Lambda, Amazon SQS, and DynamoDB to build an event-driven data processing system. Furthermore, I have come to appreciate the role of an AI Agent in assisting with the programming and deployment of real-world applications on a cloud computing platform.
Author: Kieu Minh Quang
References: AWS – Build AWS Marketplace SaaS metering with the metering agent skill

BLOG 3: INTEGRATING PROCUREMENT WORKFLOWS WITH AWS MARKETPLACE VIA APIS Building an Automated Software Procurement System Using AWS Marketplace APIs and Serverless Architecture Hello everyone! Today, I’d like to share an interesting AWS solution for integrating software procurement workflows into enterprise systems. By leveraging AWS Marketplace APIs, organizations can search for products, manage agreements, subscribe to services, and track costs directly from their own internal platforms—eliminating the need to constantly access the AWS Management Console.
3.3.1 The Challenge In large enterprises, the process of searching for, selecting, and managing software typically involves multiple departments, such as IT, Finance, and Procurement.
If every task must be performed manually within the AWS Management Console, users end up spending significant time searching for products, comparing prices, managing contracts, and consolidating cost reports.
Consequently, enterprises require a solution that integrates these procurement activities into their existing operational workflows.
3.3.2 The AWS Solution Figure 3.3: Serverless architecture of the MP-Buyer Portal integrated with AWS Marketplace APIs.
AWS offers the “MP-Buyer Portal”—a serverless reference application designed to integrate AWS Marketplace functionalities into a custom web interface.
The solution utilizes the following key components:
AWS Marketplace Discovery API: Facilitates product searches, filtering, and the comparison of software options. AWS Marketplace Agreement API: Manages contracts, pricing information, and product subscription workflows. Amazon CloudFront and Amazon S3: Handle the distribution and hosting of the web interface. Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda: Manage incoming requests and process procurement-related operations. - Amazon DynamoDB: Stores and synchronizes contract data to facilitate faster report retrieval. Amazon Cognito: Handles user authentication and secures system access. Amazon EventBridge: Automatically triggers the data synchronization process every 6 hours. Additionally, the system can incorporate Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock to analyze data, generate reports, and provide cost-optimization recommendations.
3.3.3 Benefits and Security A key highlight of this solution is its ability to integrate procurement processes into internal systems, making it more convenient for users to search for products, manage subscriptions, and track expenses.
Furthermore, the serverless architecture reduces the need for infrastructure management and optimizes costs during periods of system inactivity.
Regarding security, the solution utilizes Amazon Cognito for user authentication, HTTPS via CloudFront, private S3 buckets, and the principle of least privilege (via IAM) to restrict access. For actual deployments, it is also recommended to incorporate AWS WAF, implement CORS restrictions, and configure CloudWatch alerts.
3.3.4 Personal Assessment & Conclusion In my view, this is a highly useful solution for businesses looking to automate procurement and software management processes. Leveraging AWS Marketplace APIs minimizes manual tasks and enables the integration of purchasing functionality directly into the systems a business already uses.
Through this article, I have gained a better understanding of how to combine Amazon CloudFront, API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, and Cognito to build a complete serverless application. It has also provided an opportunity to delve deeper into API integration, data management, and security within a cloud computing architecture.
Author: Kieu Minh Quang
References: AWS – How You Can Embed Procurement into Your Workflows with AWS Marketplace APIs

title: Create a gateway endpoint
content:
Step 1 – Create the VPC Open VPC Console → Your VPCs → Create VPC. Choose VPC only, name techvina-vpc, IPv4 CIDR 10.20.0.0/16, tenancy Default. Select Create VPC. Under Actions → Edit VPC settings, enable DNS resolution and DNS hostnames. Step 2 – Create three subnets Under VPC → Subnets → Create subnet, select the VPC and create:
Subnet Availability Zone IPv4 CIDR Purpose techvina-public-a ap-southeast-1a 10.20.1.0/24 EC2 techvina-private-a ap-southeast-1a 10.20.11.0/24 RDS techvina-private-b ap-southeast-1b 10.20.12.0/24 RDS For the public subnet, enable auto-assign public IPv4. Leave it disabled for both private subnets.
Step 3 – Internet Gateway and routing Go to Internet gateways → Create internet gateway, name techvina-igw, and Attach to VPC. Select Route tables → Create route table, name it techvina-public-rt, and select the VPC. Add route 0.0.0.0/0 → techvina-igw under Routes → Edit routes. Associate the route table with techvina-public-a. Create techvina-private-rt for both private subnets. Keep only the local VPC route; do not add a default Internet route to private subnets. Step 4 – Validate Inspect VPC → Resource map: the public subnet has an IGW route while the private subnets have no Internet default route. Record the VPC ID and all Subnet IDs for EC2 and RDS.

title: Introduction
content:
Introduction to the System In this workshop, we will build the AWS infrastructure required to deploy a mobile phone e-commerce web application for customers and administrators. Customers can browse and search for products, register, sign in, and place orders. Administrators can manage products, images, and orders according to the features implemented by the development team.
The application consists of three common components:
Frontend (user interface): ReactJS displays the website in a browser. Backend (application server): Java Spring Boot exposes REST APIs and processes requests from the frontend. Database: MySQL stores products, users, and orders according to the application’s data model. Instead of running these components only on local computers, we will deploy them on AWS so that the website can be accessed and tested over the Internet.
Workshop Overview 1. Objectives By the end of this workshop, participants should be able to:
Create and configure a network environment with Amazon VPC and manage access with AWS IAM. Deploy Spring Boot on Amazon EC2 and connect it to Amazon RDS for MySQL. Upload the production ReactJS build to Amazon S3 and deliver the frontend through Amazon CloudFront. Store product images in the same S3 bucket as the Frontend. Integrate Amazon Cognito for user registration, sign-in, and JWT authentication. Observe server and application activity with Amazon CloudWatch. Validate end-to-end browser, API, database, and image flows, then clean up lab resources. 2. System Architecture AWS Services and Their Roles
Service Role in the project Amazon VPC Provides networking for EC2 and RDS and separates public and private subnets. AWS IAM Grants deployment permissions and EC2 instance-role permissions as needed. Amazon EC2 Runs Spring Boot on port 8080 and Nginx HTTPS on port 443. Amazon RDS for MySQL Hosts and manages the application’s MySQL database. Amazon S3 Uses one bucket for the ReactJS build and product images, and another for Backend Artifacts. Amazon CloudFront Delivers frontend/images using S3 OAC and forwards /api/* to the DuckDNS HTTPS origin. Amazon Cognito Supports registration, sign-in, and JWT authentication. Amazon CloudWatch Collects metrics and logs and enables operational alarms. How the components work together
Website access: Users open the CloudFront HTTPS URL. CloudFront retrieves the ReactJS assets from S3 and returns them to the browser. Product images: The browser requests product images through CloudFront, which retrieves the corresponding objects from the Frontend bucket. API requests: ReactJS sends /api/* requests to CloudFront; CloudFront forwards these requests to Spring Boot on EC2. Database access: Spring Boot connects to RDS MySQL over the private VPC network to query and update data. Sign-in: Users authenticate with Cognito. After sign-in, the frontend includes a JWT in protected API requests; Spring Boot validates the token before processing the requests. Monitoring: CloudWatch provides metrics and logs to help operators inspect service health. 3. Deployment Scope and Resources Resource group Proposed workshop setup Networking 1 VPC; 1 Public Subnet for EC2; 2 Private Subnets in different Availability Zones for RDS; Internet Gateway; Route Tables; Security Groups. Compute 1 EC2 instance running Spring Boot, with an EBS volume. Database 1 Single-AZ RDS MySQL instance and 1 DB Subnet Group with 2 Private Subnets. Storage 2 S3 buckets: Frontend (including images) and Backend Artifacts. Content delivery 1 CloudFront distribution with appropriate origins and behaviors for frontend, images, and API requests. Authentication A Cognito User Pool and App Client integrated into the application. Permissions IAM Role/Policy for EC2 and the permissions needed to use S3. Monitoring CloudWatch metrics, logs, and an alarm for validation. 4. Workshop Implementation Steps 5.2 – Prerequisites: Prepare the AWS account, deployment permissions, application source/build artifacts, and required tools. 5.3 – IAM and VPC Setup: Create a Role/Policy, VPC, Subnets, Internet Gateway, Route Tables, and Security Groups. 5.4 – Amazon RDS Deployment: Create a DB Subnet Group, RDS MySQL instance, and network rules allowing database connections from EC2 only. 5.5 – Backend Deployment on EC2: Launch an instance, install Java, deploy Spring Boot, configure RDS connectivity, and test the API. 5.6 – Amazon S3 Deployment: Create two private S3 buckets and manually upload product images to the Frontend bucket. 5.7 – CloudFront and System Integration: Configure DuckDNS/Nginx HTTPS, CloudFront origins, /api/* routing, the SPA Function and Cognito callbacks; manually build and deploy the frontend. 5.8 – CI/CD, Monitoring and Testing: Configure GitHub Actions OIDC, automate frontend/backend deployments, and verify CloudWatch metrics, logs, alarms, and end-to-end flows. 5.9 – Resource Clean-up: Remove lab resources in the appropriate order to avoid unnecessary charges. 5. Security Requirements S3: Keep buckets private and use CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) to deliver content from S3. RDS: Deploy the database in Private Subnets, disable public access, and allow MySQL traffic on port 3306 only from the EC2 Security Group. EC2 and IAM: Use an IAM Role instead of embedding access keys in application code, and restrict Internet-facing ports. Use HTTPS port 443 between CloudFront and EC2 Nginx with a valid certificate; do not expose Spring Boot port 8080 publicly. Authentication: Spring Boot must validate JWTs and user authorization for protected API operations. Monitoring: Observe operational metrics, application logs, and alarms during testing. 6. Database The backend successfully reads and writes data in RDS MySQL. Images Product images are delivered from S3 via CloudFront. Sign-in Users authenticate with Cognito and access protected APIs with valid JWTs. Security RDS is not directly accessible from the Internet; S3 objects are not publicly readable through direct bucket access. title: Prepare the environment
content:
Step 1 – Create a DB Subnet Group Step 1.1 – Open the DB Subnet Group creation page In the AWS Management Console, select Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1. Open the RDS service. In the left navigation menu, choose Subnet groups. Select Create DB subnet group. Step 1.2 – Enter the Subnet Group details Under Subnet group details, complete the following fields:
AWS Console field Value Name techvina-db-subnet-group Description TechVina private database subnets VPC techvina-vpc Once the VPC is selected, the Availability Zones and Subnets controls below show resources belonging to techvina-vpc.
Step 1.3 – Select two Availability Zones Under Add subnets:
Open the Availability Zones dropdown (Choose an availability zone). Select ap-southeast-1a. Open the dropdown again and select ap-southeast-1b. Confirm that both ap-southeast-1a and ap-southeast-1b appear as selected tags. Step 1.4 – Select the two private subnets Open the Subnets dropdown (Select subnets). Select techvina-private-a – CIDR 10.20.11.0/24. Open Subnets again and select techvina-private-b – CIDR 10.20.12.0/24. Verify the Subnets selected (2) table at the bottom of the page: Availability Zone Subnet name CIDR block ap-southeast-1a techvina-private-a 10.20.11.0/24 ap-southeast-1b techvina-private-b 10.20.12.0/24 Do not select techvina-public-a; the database will be deployed in private subnets.
The Console notice “For Multi-AZ DB clusters, you must select 3 subnets in 3 different Availability Zones” applies to Multi-AZ DB Clusters. Step 2 creates a Single DB Instance, for which two subnets in two different Availability Zones are appropriate.
Step 1.5 – Create and verify the DB Subnet Group Click Create in the bottom-right corner. In RDS → Subnet groups, open techvina-db-subnet-group. Confirm it belongs to techvina-vpc and includes techvina-private-a and techvina-private-b. Step 2 – Create an Amazon RDS MySQL database Step 2.1 – Open the Create database page In the AWS Console, navigate to Aurora and RDS → Databases. Select Create database → Full configuration. Under Engine options → Engine type, choose MySQL (not Aurora). Under Choose a database creation method, choose Full configuration. Step 2.2 – Choose the template and MySQL version Under Templates, select Dev/Test. Under Availability and durability → Deployment options, choose Single-AZ DB instance deployment (1 instance). Under Settings → Edition, keep MySQL Community. Under Engine version, select MySQL 8.4.11 from the version list shown in the Console. Leave Enable RDS Extended Support unchecked. Step 2.3 – Set the DB identifier and master credentials Under Settings → DB instance identifier, change database-1 to techvina-mysql.
Under Credentials Settings, configure:
AWS Console field Value Master username admin Credentials management Self managed Auto generate password Unchecked Master password A strong password you create Confirm master password Re-enter the same password Expand Additional credentials settings → Database authentication options and keep Password authentication. Store the master password privately for use when importing MySQL data.
Step 2.4 – Choose a DB instance class Under Instance configuration → DB instance class:
Select Burstable classes (includes t classes). Open Instance type and select db.t3.micro. Step 2.5 – Configure storage Under Storage, set:
AWS Console field Value Storage type General Purpose SSD (gp3) Allocated storage 20 GiB Provisioned IOPS Keep the Console default if automatically populated Storage throughput Keep the Console default if automatically populated If Additional storage configuration is shown, expand it and disable Enable storage autoscaling to keep storage capacity fixed during the lab.
Step 2.6 – Configure Connectivity Under Connectivity, configure the fields in order:
AWS Console field Value Compute resource Don’t connect to an EC2 compute resource Network type IPv4 Virtual private cloud (VPC) techvina-vpc DB subnet group techvina-db-subnet-group Public access No VPC security group (firewall) Choose existing Existing VPC security groups techvina-rds-sg only Availability Zone No preference Create an RDS Proxy Unchecked Certificate authority Keep the displayed default rds-ca-rsa2048-g1, if shown Change Virtual private cloud (VPC) from Default VPC to techvina-vpc before selecting the DB subnet group. Under Existing VPC security groups, remove the default selection and add techvina-rds-sg.
Step 2.7 – Configure Monitoring Under Monitoring:
Select Database Insights – Standard. If Collect detailed database and per-query metrics is checked, leave Retention period = 7 days. You may uncheck it if detailed query metrics are not needed. Expand Additional monitoring settings. Uncheck Enable Enhanced monitoring. Under Log exports, leave all log types unchecked during initial creation. Standard CloudWatch metrics such as CPUUtilization, FreeStorageSpace, and DatabaseConnections remain available after database creation.
Step 2.8 – Configure Additional configuration Expand Additional configuration and set or verify:
AWS Console field Value Initial database name phone_store DB parameter group default.mysql8.4 Option group default:mysql-8-4 Enable encryption Enabled AWS KMS key (default) aws/rds Enable automated backup Enabled Backup retention period 7 days Backup window No preference Enable replication in another AWS Region Unchecked Enable auto minor version upgrade Enabled Maintenance window No preference Enable deletion protection Unchecked Keep Capacity reservations set to No capacity reservations. Tags are optional.
Step 2.9 – Review and create the database Scroll to Estimated monthly costs and review the estimate for the selected settings. Verify: db.t3.micro, 20 GiB, Single-AZ, VPC techvina-vpc, Subnet group techvina-db-subnet-group, Public access = No, Security Group techvina-rds-sg. Select Create database. In Aurora and RDS → Databases, open techvina-mysql and check Status = Available. Step 3 – Record the connection details Open the DB instance Connectivity & security tab. Record the endpoint (for example techvina-mysql.xxxxx.ap-southeast-1.rds.amazonaws.com) and Port 3306.
RDS_ENDPOINT=<YOUR_RDS_ENDPOINT> DB_URL=jdbc:mysql://<YOUR_RDS_ENDPOINT>:3306/phone_store DB_USERNAME=<APP_DB_USERNAME> DB_PASSWORD=<APP_DB_PASSWORD> Expected result: RDS MySQL stays private and accepts port 3306 only from the EC2 Security Group.

title: Configure CloudFront Origins, HTTPS and Behaviors
content:
Step 1 – Create a CloudFront distribution and S3 origin Open CloudFront → Distributions → Create distribution. Use the description techvina-cloudfront and select techvina-frontend-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID> as the first origin. Choose the S3 REST endpoint, not the website endpoint. Select Origin access control settings (recommended), create an OAC, and choose Sign requests. Set the Default (*) cache behavior to Redirect HTTP to HTTPS and CachingOptimized. Set Default root object to index.html. Create the distribution and record its Distribution ID and domain (dxxxxxxxxxxxxx.cloudfront.net). The actual TechVina deployment uses the distribution techvina-cloudfront and domain d3mmtr3bxttvgc.cloudfront.net. The finished distribution has two origins: one S3 origin serving the frontend and images, and one HTTPS custom origin for Spring Boot. The backend origin is added in Step 4.
Step 2 – Grant private S3 access through OAC Open Origins, select the frontend S3 origin, and verify that OAC is configured. If AWS Console offers Copy policy / Go to S3 bucket permissions, apply a bucket policy based on this template, substituting the Account ID and Distribution ID: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowCloudFrontReadFrontend", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "cloudfront.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::techvina-frontend-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>/*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "AWS:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudfront::<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>:distribution/<CF_DISTRIBUTION_ID>" } } } ] } Keep Block all public access enabled. Test an image already uploaded in 5.6.2: https://<CF_DOMAIN>/images/products/xiaomi/xiaomi-series/xiaomi-15/image_1262703568.webp The image should load through CloudFront while a direct unauthenticated S3 object URL remains inaccessible.
Step 3 – Configure DuckDNS and HTTPS for EC2 Step 3.1 – Create the DuckDNS hostname In DuckDNS, create a subdomain using the pattern techvina-api-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>. Point the hostname to the Public IPv4 of techvina-ec2-backend and save it. The hostname used in the actual deployment is: techvina-api-668668940018.duckdns.org Connect to EC2 using Session Manager as ubuntu and verify the IPv4 resolution: getent ahostsv4 techvina-api-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>.duckdns.org | head -n 1 The returned address must match the instance public IPv4. Using a dynamic DNS hostname avoids configuring CloudFront with a temporary EC2 public DNS name that can change after Stop/Start.
Step 3.2 – Set up automatic DuckDNS updates Create a root-only token file:
sudo install -d -m 700 /etc/techvina/duckdns sudo nano /etc/techvina/duckdns/token sudo chmod 600 /etc/techvina/duckdns/token Enter your own DuckDNS token. Do not include it in the workshop, GitHub, logs, or screenshots.
Create /usr/local/sbin/techvina-duckdns-update.sh:
sudo nano /usr/local/sbin/techvina-duckdns-update.sh #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail DOMAIN="techvina-api-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>" TOKEN_FILE="/etc/techvina/duckdns/token" TOKEN="$(tr -d '\r\n' < "$TOKEN_FILE")" if [[ ! "$TOKEN" =~ ^[a-zA-Z0-9-]+$ ]]; then echo "Invalid DuckDNS token" >&2 exit 1 fi RESPONSE="$( printf 'url = "https://www.duckdns.org/update?domains=%s&token=%s&ip="\n' "$DOMAIN" "$TOKEN" \ | curl --fail --silent --show-error --max-time 20 --config - )" if [[ "$RESPONSE" == "OK" ]]; then echo "DuckDNS update OK" else echo "DuckDNS update failed" >&2 exit 1 fi Replace <AWS_ACCOUNT_ID> with your account ID, then make the script executable and test it:
sudo chmod 700 /usr/local/sbin/techvina-duckdns-update.sh sudo /usr/local/sbin/techvina-duckdns-update.sh Verified output: DuckDNS update OK.
Create /etc/systemd/system/techvina-duckdns-update.service:
[Unit] Description=TechVina DuckDNS IP Update Wants=network-online.target After=network-online.target [Service] Type=oneshot User=root ExecStart=/usr/local/sbin/techvina-duckdns-update.sh Create /etc/systemd/system/techvina-duckdns-update.timer:
[Unit] Description=TechVina DuckDNS Update Timer [Timer] OnBootSec=1min OnUnitActiveSec=5min AccuracySec=30s Unit=techvina-duckdns-update.service [Install] WantedBy=timers.target Verify, reload systemd, and enable the timer:
sudo systemd-analyze verify /etc/systemd/system/techvina-duckdns-update.service /etc/systemd/system/techvina-duckdns-update.timer sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now techvina-duckdns-update.timer systemctl list-timers --all | grep techvina-duckdns Step 3.3 – Set up Nginx and Let’s Encrypt The EC2 Security Group configured in 5.3.2 must allow TCP 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 for HTTP-01 certificate issuance/renewal, and TCP 443 from the CloudFront origin-facing prefix list. Spring Boot continues to run on 127.0.0.1:8080; port 8080 is not exposed publicly.
Install Nginx and Certbot:
sudo apt update sudo apt install -y nginx certbot python3-certbot-nginx Create /etc/nginx/sites-available/techvina-backend:
server { listen 80; server_name techvina-api-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>.duckdns.org; location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; } } Replace the Account ID, activate Nginx, and issue the certificate:
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/techvina-backend /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/techvina-backend sudo nginx -t sudo systemctl reload nginx sudo certbot --nginx -d techvina-api-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>.duckdns.org Choose Redirect HTTP to HTTPS when prompted. Certbot adds the TLS configuration and manages automated renewal. Verify:
sudo nginx -t sudo systemctl status nginx --no-pager Before restricting origin port 443 to CloudFront, the actual deployment verified https://techvina-api-668668940018.duckdns.org/actuator/health returned HTTP 200 and {"status":"UP"}. Requests to HTTP port 80 redirected with 301 to HTTPS.
Step 4 – Create the backend HTTPS origin Under the distribution, open Origins → Create origin:
Field Value Origin domain techvina-api-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>.duckdns.org (without https://) Origin type Custom origin Name techvina-ec2-backend Protocol HTTPS only HTTPS port 443 Minimum Origin SSL protocol TLSv1.2 Origin path Empty Origin IP address type IPv4-only Keep the default timeouts, do not add secret custom headers, and choose Create origin. The Origin domain must match the hostname on the valid TLS certificate.
Step 5 – Create the /api/* behavior Open Behaviors → Create behavior:
Field Value Path pattern /api/* Origin techvina-ec2-backend Viewer protocol policy Redirect HTTP to HTTPS Allowed HTTP methods GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, POST, PATCH, DELETE Cache HTTP OPTIONS Not selected Cache policy CachingDisabled Origin request policy AllViewerExceptHostHeader Response headers policy None AllViewerExceptHostHeader forwards the required headers (including Authorization), cookies and query strings while using the DuckDNS host at the origin, which is appropriate for TLS and Nginx.
Verify the ordered behaviors:
Precedence Path pattern Origin 0 /api/* techvina-ec2-backend 1 Default (*) Frontend S3 + images Test:
https://<CF_DOMAIN>/api/san-pham/noi-bat Actual result: HTTP 200 with JSON for four featured products. Dynamic API responses are not cached by CloudFront.
Step 6 – Create a CloudFront Function for React Router Routes such as /login and /san-pham/21/21 are handled by React Router, not by individual S3 files. Open CloudFront → Functions → Create function:
Function name: techvina-spa-routing Runtime: cloudfront-js-2.0 In Build (Development) replace the example code with:
function handler(event) { var request = event.request; var uri = request.uri; if ( uri === '/api' || uri.startsWith('/api/') || uri === '/images' || uri.startsWith('/images/') || uri === '/assets' || uri.startsWith('/assets/') ) { return request; } var lastSegment = uri.substring(uri.lastIndexOf('/') + 1); if (uri !== '/' && !lastSegment.includes('.')) { request.uri = '/index.html'; } return request; } Choose Save changes. Open Test in Development, simulate GET /san-pham/21/21, and choose Run test. Verify Status = Success and request.uri = "/index.html". Choose Publish → Publish function to promote the tested code to LIVE. Choose Add association, select the TechVina distribution, Event type = Viewer request, and Cache behavior = Default (*). If a replacement warning appears, first inspect Behaviors → Default (*) → Edit → Function associations to check for an existing function. Choose Add association and allow the distribution configuration to deploy. Associate the function only with Default (*), not /api/*. The function preserves /assets/..., /images/... and actual file URLs. Once the frontend is uploaded in 5.7.3, /san-pham/21/21 can render the product page instead of S3’s XML AccessDenied response.
Step 7 – Verify CloudFront routing Open https://<CF_DOMAIN>/images/products/xiaomi/xiaomi-series/xiaomi-15/image_1262703568.webp to verify image delivery from S3. Open https://<CF_DOMAIN>/api/san-pham/noi-bat to verify the Spring Boot JSON response through the HTTPS origin. Verify the S3 and techvina-ec2-backend origins and the order of /api/* and Default (*) behaviors. Once the frontend build has been deployed in 5.7.3, test /, /login, /san-pham/21/21, and /assets/.

title: Connect GitHub Actions to AWS with OIDC
content:
Step 1 – Create the GitHub OIDC Identity Provider Open AWS Console → IAM → Identity providers → Add provider.
Select OpenID Connect as the provider type.
Enter the following values:
Field Value Provider URL https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com Audience sts.amazonaws.com Select Add provider. Under Identity providers, verify that token.actions.githubusercontent.com appears with type OpenID Connect.
Step 2 – Create Two GitHub Actions IAM Roles Open IAM → Roles → Create role.
Select Web identity, choose provider token.actions.githubusercontent.com and audience sts.amazonaws.com.
Create the following two roles:
Role Purpose techvina-github-actions-frontend-role Upload the React build to S3 and create a CloudFront invalidation techvina-github-actions-backend-role Upload the JAR/deployment script to S3 and deploy to EC2 through SSM Open each role and choose Trust relationships → Edit trust policy to restrict access to the intended GitHub repository and branch.
Step 3 – Configure the Trust Policy Using the GitHub OIDC Subject The TechVina repository was created after 15 July 2026, so its GitHub OIDC token uses an immutable sub claim that includes both the Owner ID and Repository ID:
repo:<GITHUB_OWNER>@<OWNER_ID>/<REPOSITORY>@<REPO_ID>:ref:refs/heads/master For both IAM roles, open Trust relationships → Edit trust policy and enter the following JSON. Replace the values enclosed in <...> with the actual AWS account and GitHub repository values:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com", "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:<GITHUB_OWNER>@<OWNER_ID>/TechVina@<REPO_ID>:ref:refs/heads/master" } } } ] } The TechVina deployment branch is master. The StringEquals conditions restrict role assumption to the configured repository and branch.
Match the sub condition to the actual claim emitted by GitHub Actions. Older repositories may emit the earlier subject format without immutable IDs; the trust policy must use the value that the repository actually issues.
Select Update policy, and repeat for the Frontend IAM role.
Step 4 – Grant Permissions to the Frontend IAM Role Open techvina-github-actions-frontend-role. Choose Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON. Enter the following policy, replacing <AWS_ACCOUNT_ID> and <CF_DISTRIBUTION_ID> with the actual resource identifiers: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "ListFrontendBucket", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:ListBucket", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::techvina-frontend-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>" }, { "Sid": "UploadFrontendFiles", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:PutObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::techvina-frontend-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>/*" }, { "Sid": "InvalidateCloudFront", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "cloudfront:CreateInvalidation", "Resource": "arn:aws:cloudfront::<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>:distribution/<CF_DISTRIBUTION_ID>" } ] } Save the inline policy. The S3 permissions allow aws s3 sync to upload the Frontend build; the CloudFront permission is scoped to the TechVina distribution. Step 5 – Grant Permissions to the Backend IAM Role Open techvina-github-actions-backend-role. Choose Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON. Configure S3 artifact upload and SSM deployment permissions: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "UploadBackendArtifacts", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:PutObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::techvina-backend-artifacts-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>/releases/*" }, { "Sid": "RunDeployCommandOnEC2", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "ssm:SendCommand", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:ssm:ap-southeast-1::document/AWS-RunShellScript", "arn:aws:ec2:ap-southeast-1:<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>:instance/<EC2_INSTANCE_ID>" ] }, { "Sid": "ReadSSMCommandResult", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "ssm:GetCommandInvocation", "Resource": "*" } ] } Name the inline policy techvina-github-actions-backend-policy and save it. The ssm:SendCommand permission is restricted to the AWS-RunShellScript document and the designated Backend EC2 instance. Step 6 – Grant Artifact Read Permissions to the EC2 IAM Role Under IAM → Roles → techvina-ec2-ssm-role → Permissions, verify the inline policy allowing the EC2 host to download the JAR/deployment script from the Backend Artifacts bucket:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::techvina-backend-artifacts-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>/releases/*" } ] } EC2 uses the IAM instance profile attached to techvina-ec2-ssm-role when executing aws s3 cp; no AWS Access Keys are stored on the host. This role also has permissions for AWS Systems Manager management.
Step 7 – Enable GitHub Actions OIDC Permissions The two workflow files are:
.github/workflows/deploy-frontend.yml .github/workflows/deploy-backend.yml Each workflow grants permission to request an OIDC identity token:
permissions: contents: read id-token: write In the AWS authentication step, configure aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6.3.0 with the corresponding IAM role ARN:
- name: Configure AWS credentials uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6.3.0 with: role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>:role/techvina-github-actions-frontend-role aws-region: ap-southeast-1 The Backend workflow uses techvina-github-actions-backend-role instead. After configuring credentials, the workflows verify AWS identity with:
aws sts get-caller-identity Successful OIDC authentication is confirmed by the Frontend and Backend GitHub Actions runs documented in 5.8.2 and 5.8.3.

title: Create Two Amazon S3 Buckets
content:
Step 1 – Open Amazon S3 In the AWS Console, open Amazon S3 → General purpose buckets in Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1. Select Create bucket.
Step 2 – Create the Frontend and Images bucket Under General configuration, use:
Field Value AWS Region ap-southeast-1 Bucket type General purpose Bucket namespace Global namespace Bucket name techvina-frontend-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID> Object Ownership ACLs disabled (Bucket owner enforced) Block all public access Keep all enabled Bucket Versioning Disable Default encryption SSE-S3 Object Lock Disable Select Create bucket. This bucket stores the React/Vite build (index.html, assets/) and the product images (images/). Do not enable S3 static website hosting. CloudFront will use Origin Access Control (OAC) to read the private bucket.
Step 3 – Create the Backend Artifacts bucket Return to General purpose buckets → Create bucket. Retain the security settings from Step 2 and use:
techvina-backend-artifacts-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID> Select Create bucket. This bucket will store JAR files and CI/CD artifacts under releases/. Its name must match the s3:GetObject ARN attached to the EC2 Role in section 5.3.2.
Step 4 – Create the images prefix in the Frontend bucket Open techvina-frontend-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID> → Objects → Create folder. Enter images as the Folder name (without /), retain Don’t specify an encryption key to use default SSE-S3, and select Create folder.
Step 5 – Create the releases prefix in Backend Artifacts Open techvina-backend-artifacts-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID> → Objects → Create folder. Enter releases, retain default encryption, and select Create folder.
Step 6 – Verify the buckets The two buckets now contain these prefixes:
techvina-frontend-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>/ └── images/ techvina-backend-artifacts-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>/ └── releases/ Keep Block all public access = On for both buckets. The folders are S3 key prefixes; the actual images and JARs are uploaded in the Frontend/CI/CD stages of section 5.8. CloudFront S3 read permissions are configured in 5.7.1.

title: Launch EC2, Install Dependencies and Initialize RDS
content:
Step 1 – Launch the Backend EC2 instance Step 1.1 – Open the EC2 launch page Sign in to the AWS Management Console and choose Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1. Open EC2 → Instances and select Launch instances. Under Name and tags → Name, enter techvina-ec2-backend. In the Summary panel on the right, leave Number of instances = 1. Step 1.2 – Select the operating system (AMI) In Application and OS Images (Amazon Machine Image), choose Ubuntu under Quick Start. In Amazon Machine Image (AMI), select Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS published by Canonical. Verify Architecture = 64-bit (x86) (x86_64), not ARM (arm64). Step 1.3 – Select the instance type Open Instance type, then search for t3.small. Select t3.small. Verify that the instance offers 2 vCPUs and 2 GiB RAM. Step 1.4 – Configure the key pair Under Key pair (login), open Key pair name. Choose Proceed without a key pair (Not recommended). This workshop uses AWS Systems Manager Session Manager instead of SSH to access the instance. Step 1.5 – Configure network settings Under Network settings, click Edit to expand the fields.
Set the following values:
AWS Console field Value VPC techvina-vpc Subnet techvina-public-a Auto-assign public IP Enable Firewall (security groups) Select existing security group Common security groups / Security groups techvina-ec2-sg If Create security group is selected, switch to Select existing security group; do not create a new launch-wizard-* group.
Verify that techvina-ec2-sg, created in section 5.3.2, permits TCP 443 from the CloudFront origin-facing prefix list and TCP 80 for HTTPS certificate issuance/renewal.
Do not add an inbound SSH (22) from Anywhere (0.0.0.0/0) rule.
Step 1.6 – Configure storage Under Configure storage, keep one root volume. Change the default 8 GiB to 20 GiB. Choose Volume type = gp3. Do not add a second EBS volume or an S3/EFS/FSx file system. Step 1.7 – Configure advanced details Expand Advanced details. Under IAM instance profile, select techvina-ec2-ssm-role created in section 5.3.2. Leave unrelated fields at their defaults and verify these settings: Field Value Shutdown behavior Stop Detailed CloudWatch monitoring Disable Credit specification Standard Purchasing option None (On-Demand) Metadata accessible Enabled Metadata version V2 only (token required) User data Leave blank Step 1.8 – Review and launch In Summary, verify 1 instance, Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS, t3.small, techvina-ec2-sg, and 20 GiB gp3. Recheck VPC techvina-vpc, Subnet techvina-public-a, Auto-assign public IP = Enable, and IAM instance profile techvina-ec2-ssm-role. Click Launch instance. Open EC2 → Instances and select techvina-ec2-backend. Wait for Instance state = Running and Status check = 2/2 checks passed. Record the Instance ID, Public IPv4 address and Public IPv4 DNS from the instance details; they will be used in later deployment steps. Step 2 – Connect to EC2 and install tools Step 2.1 – Connect using AWS Systems Manager Go to EC2 → Instances and select techvina-ec2-backend. Click Connect. Under Choose how to connect, select SSM Session Manager, then click Connect. A browser-based terminal opens without an SSH key or inbound port 22. Check the current user:
whoami ssm-user Check the operating system:
cat /etc/os-release PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS" NAME="Ubuntu" VERSION_ID="24.04" VERSION="24.04.5 LTS (Noble Numbat)" VERSION_CODENAME=noble ID=ubuntu ID_LIKE=debian HOME_URL="https://www.ubuntu.com/" SUPPORT_URL="https://help.ubuntu.com/" BUG_REPORT_URL="https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/" PRIVACY_POLICY_URL="https://www.ubuntu.com/legal/terms-and-policies/privacy-policy" UBUNTU_CODENAME=noble LOGO=ubuntu-logo Verify administrator privileges:
sudo whoami root Step 2.2 – Refresh Ubuntu package indexes sudo apt update The final output was:
Fetched 38.2 MB in 6s (5902 kB/s) Reading package lists... Done Building dependency tree... Done Reading state information... Done 40 packages can be upgraded. Run 'apt list --upgradable' to see them. The package indexes were refreshed. The notice about 40 upgradable packages is not an error.
Step 2.3 – Install and verify Java 21 sudo apt install -y openjdk-21-jdk-headless The installation completed with these messages:
Running kernel seems to be up-to-date. No services need to be restarted. No containers need to be restarted. Verify Java:
java -version openjdk version "21.0.13.0.3" 2026-10-24 OpenJDK Runtime Environment (build 21.0.13.0.3+1-1-24.04.1-Ubuntu) OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM (build 21.0.13.0.3+1-1-24.04.1-Ubuntu, mixed mode, sharing) Step 2.4 – Check Git git --version git version 2.43.0 Git was preinstalled in the Ubuntu AMI used in this deployment.
Step 2.5 – Install MySQL Client Check whether the MySQL client is available:
mysql --version sh: 8: mysql: not found Install the client without installing a MySQL server on EC2:
sudo apt install -y mysql-client The last installation messages included:
Setting up mysql-client-core-8.0 (8.0.46-0ubuntu0.24.04.5) ... Setting up mysql-client-8.0 (8.0.46-0ubuntu0.24.04.5) ... Setting up mysql-client (8.0.46-0ubuntu0.24.04.5) ... Processing triggers for man-db (2.12.0-4build2) ... Verify the version:
mysql --version mysql Ver 8.0.46-0ubuntu0.24.04.5 for Linux on x86_64 ((Ubuntu)) Step 2.6 – Install AWS CLI v2 Check AWS CLI:
aws --version sh: 11: aws: not found Verify Snap is available:
snap version snap 2.77.1+ubuntu24.04 snapd 2.77.1+ubuntu24.04 series 16 ubuntu 24.04 kernel 7.0.0-1014-aws architecture amd64 Install AWS CLI v2:
sudo snap install aws-cli --classic aws-cli (v2/stable) 2.35.21 from Amazon Web Services (aws✓) installed Verify the installation:
aws --version aws-cli/2.35.21 Python/3.14.6 Linux/7.0.0-1014-aws exe/x86_64.ubuntu.24 Step 2.7 – Verify the EC2 IAM Role aws sts get-caller-identity The output confirms that AWS CLI receives temporary credentials through the techvina-ec2-ssm-role instance profile:
{ "UserId": "<ROLE_SESSION_ID>:<INSTANCE_ID>", "Account": "<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>", "Arn": "arn:aws:sts::<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>:assumed-role/techvina-ec2-ssm-role/<INSTANCE_ID>" } No aws configure command or long-lived Access Keys are required on EC2.
Step 2.8 – Check disk capacity df -h / /dev/root 19G 2.7G 16G 15% / The root filesystem provides approximately 19 GiB of usable space on the configured 20 GiB gp3 EBS volume.
Step 3 – Connect to Amazon RDS and import data Step 3.1 – Obtain the RDS Endpoint Open Amazon RDS → Databases → techvina-mysql. Select Connectivity & security and locate Endpoint & port. Verify Port = 3306, Publicly accessible = No, VPC = techvina-vpc, and Security group = techvina-rds-sg. In the EC2 terminal, set RDS_ENDPOINT to the endpoint assigned to the RDS instance in the current AWS account:
export RDS_ENDPOINT='YOUR_RDS_ENDPOINT' Step 3.2 – Connect using MySQL Client mysql -h "$RDS_ENDPOINT" -P 3306 -u admin -p --ssl-mode=REQUIRED --connect-timeout=10 Enter the RDS password at the Enter password: prompt. A successful connection opens MySQL Monitor with a mysql> prompt. The verified database engine was MySQL 8.4.11.
List the databases:
SHOW DATABASES; +--------------------+ | Database | +--------------------+ | information_schema | | mysql | | performance_schema | | phone_store | | sys | +--------------------+ 5 rows in set (0.02 sec) Check the tables before importing:
SHOW TABLES FROM phone_store; Empty set (0.01 sec) Exit MySQL Monitor:
exit; Bye Step 3.3 – Prepare the repository on EC2 Switch from ssm-user to ubuntu:
sudo -iu ubuntu Terminal prompt:
ubuntu@ip-10-20-1-19:~$ Set the endpoint again in the ubuntu login shell (the ssm-user variable is not carried over):
export RDS_ENDPOINT='YOUR_RDS_ENDPOINT' Create the project directory:
mkdir -p ~/projects Enter the directory:
cd ~/projects Clone the TechVina GitHub repository (use your own fork if its owner differs):
git clone https://github.com/TaiHoang69/TechVina.git Cloning into 'TechVina'... remote: Enumerating objects: 307, done. remote: Counting objects: 100% (307/307), done. remote: Compressing objects: 100% (271/271), done. remote: Total 307 (delta 21), reused 307 (delta 21), pack-reused 0 (from 0) Receiving objects: 100% (307/307), 2.38 MiB | 34.79 MiB/s, done. Resolving deltas: 100% (21/21), done. Inspect the source directory:
ls -la ~/projects/TechVina total 32 drwxrwxr-x 7 ubuntu ubuntu 4096 Nov 12 14:32 . drwxrwxr-x 3 ubuntu ubuntu 4096 Nov 12 14:32 .. drwxrwxr-x 8 ubuntu ubuntu 4096 Nov 12 14:32 .git drwxrwxr-x 5 ubuntu ubuntu 4096 Nov 12 14:32 .github -rw-rw-r-- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 931 Nov 12 14:32 .gitignore drwxrwxr-x 4 ubuntu ubuntu 4096 Nov 12 14:32 backend drwxrwxr-x 4 ubuntu ubuntu 4096 Nov 12 14:32 database drwxrwxr-x 4 ubuntu ubuntu 4096 Nov 12 14:32 frontend Step 3.4 – Inspect the SQL dump Locate SQL files:
find ~/projects/TechVina/database -type f -name "*.sql" /home/ubuntu/projects/TechVina/database/full/phone_store.sql Inspect the first 40 lines:
head -n 40 ~/projects/TechVina/database/full/phone_store.sql The beginning confirms a MySQL 8.0.44 dump of phone_store using utf8mb4:
-- MySQL dump 10.13 Distrib 8.0.44, for Win64 (x86_64) -- Host: localhost Database: phone_store -- Server version 8.0.44 CREATE DATABASE /*!32312 IF NOT EXISTS*/ `phone_store` /*!40100 DEFAULT CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci */ /*!80016 DEFAULT ENCRYPTION='N' */; USE `phone_store`; -- Table structure for table `anh` DROP TABLE IF EXISTS `anh`; Look for statements that might require additional permissions on RDS:
grep -niEm 20 'DEFINER[[:space:]]*=|GTID_PURGED|SQL_LOG_BIN|CREATE[[:space:]]+USER|DROP[[:space:]]+DATABASE' ~/projects/TechVina/database/full/phone_store.sql No matches were returned for this SQL file.
Step 3.5 – Import the SQL dump into RDS Import only after verifying that the destination database has no tables:
mysql -h "$RDS_ENDPOINT" -P 3306 -u admin -p --ssl-mode=REQUIRED --default-character-set=utf8mb4 phone_store < ~/projects/TechVina/database/full/phone_store.sql Enter the password for the MySQL admin account when prompted. A successful import displays no confirmation message and returns to the Linux prompt.
Step 3.6 – Verify table counts mysql -h "$RDS_ENDPOINT" -P 3306 -u admin -p --ssl-mode=REQUIRED phone_store -e "SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_tables FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'phone_store';" +--------------+ | total_tables | +--------------+ | 36 | +--------------+ List the tables:
mysql -h "$RDS_ENDPOINT" -P 3306 -u admin -p --ssl-mode=REQUIRED phone_store -e "SHOW TABLES;" +---------------------------+ | Tables_in_phone_store | +---------------------------+ | anh | | cauhinhdungluong | | chitietdonhang | | chitietgiamgia | | chitietgiohang | | chitietphieunhap | | chitietthongso | | danhmuc | | diachi | | donhang | | giamgia | | giohang | | hang | | khachhang | | kho | | lichsugia | | lichsutrangthainhacungcap | | mausac | | nhacungcap | | nhanvien | | nhomthongso | | phienban | | phieunhap | | ram | | refreshtoken | | rom | | sanpham | | thanhtoan | | thitruong | | thongsokythuat | | tonkho | | trangthaidonhang | | trangthainhacungcap | | trangthaiphieunhap | | vaitro | | video | +---------------------------+ Step 3.7 – Verify product data mysql -h "$RDS_ENDPOINT" -P 3306 -u admin -p --ssl-mode=REQUIRED phone_store -e "SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_products FROM sanpham;" +----------------+ | total_products | +----------------+ | 24 | +----------------+ Step 4 – Build the Backend and prepare environment variables Step 4.1 – Inspect Backend source files ls -la ~/projects/TechVina/backend total 32 drwxrwxr-x 4 ubuntu ubuntu 4096 Nov 12 14:32 . drwxrwxr-x 7 ubuntu ubuntu 4096 Nov 12 14:32 .. -rw-rw-r-- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 1984 Nov 12 14:32 .classpath -rw-rw-r-- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 930 Nov 12 14:32 .env.example -rw-rw-r-- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 684 Nov 12 14:32 .project drwxrwxr-x 2 ubuntu ubuntu 4096 Nov 12 14:32 .settings -rw-rw-r-- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 3314 Nov 12 14:32 pom.xml drwxrwxr-x 3 ubuntu ubuntu 4096 Nov 12 14:32 src The pom.xml file identifies Apache Maven as the build tool.
Step 4.2 – Install Apache Maven Check Maven:
mvn -version Command 'mvn' not found, but can be installed with: sudo apt install maven Install Maven:
sudo apt install -y maven The end of the installation output included:
Setting up libmaven3-core-java (3.8.7-2) ... Setting up maven (3.8.7-2) ... update-alternatives: using /usr/share/maven/bin/mvn to provide /usr/bin/mvn (mvn) in auto mode Verify Maven and its Java Runtime:
mvn -version Apache Maven 3.8.7 Maven home: /usr/share/maven Java version: 21.0.13.0.3, vendor: Ubuntu, runtime: /usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk-amd64 Default locale: en, platform encoding: UTF-8 OS name: "linux", version: "7.0.0-1014-aws", arch: "amd64", family: "unix" Step 4.3 – Build the Spring Boot Backend mvn -f ~/projects/TechVina/backend/pom.xml -DskipTests package Final output:
[INFO] Replacing main artifact /home/ubuntu/projects/TechVina/backend/target/backend-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar with repackaged archive, adding nested dependencies in BOOT-INF/. [INFO] The original artifact has been renamed to /home/ubuntu/projects/TechVina/backend/target/backend-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar.original [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------ [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------ [INFO] Total time: 34.850 s [INFO] Finished at: 2026-11-12T14:45:25Z [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Verify the generated JAR:
ls -lh ~/projects/TechVina/backend/target/*.jar -rw-rw-r-- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 63M Nov 12 14:45 /home/ubuntu/projects/TechVina/backend/target/backend-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar Step 4.4 – Inspect Spring Boot configuration Read the environment template:
cat ~/projects/TechVina/backend/.env.example The template defines these variables:
DB_URL=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/phone_store DB_USERNAME=YOUR_DB_USERNAME DB_PASSWORD=YOUR_DB_PASSWORD JWT_SECRET=YOUR_JWT_SECRET COGNITO_ISSUER_URI=https://cognito-idp.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/ap-southeast-1_XXXXXXXXX COGNITO_CLIENT_ID=YOUR_COGNITO_CLIENT_ID COGNITO_DOMAIN=https://YOUR_DOMAIN.auth.ap-southeast-1.amazoncognito.com Identify the application configuration file:
ls -la ~/projects/TechVina/backend/src/main/resources -rw-rw-r-- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 1801 Nov 12 14:32 application.properties Read its content:
cat ~/projects/TechVina/backend/src/main/resources/application.properties Relevant Spring Boot configuration properties:
spring.datasource.url=${DB_URL} spring.datasource.username=${DB_USERNAME} spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD} spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate jwt.secret=${JWT_SECRET} spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri=${COGNITO_ISSUER_URI} cognito.client-id=${COGNITO_CLIENT_ID} cognito.domain=${COGNITO_DOMAIN} With ddl-auto=validate, Hibernate validates entities against the imported schema rather than creating tables.
Step 4.5 – Create .env with restricted permissions Confirm Git ignores .env:
git -C ~/projects/TechVina check-ignore -v backend/.env .gitignore:17:/backend/.env backend/.env Copy the template to .env, readable and writable only by ubuntu:
install -m 600 ~/projects/TechVina/backend/.env.example ~/projects/TechVina/backend/.env Verify permissions:
ls -l ~/projects/TechVina/backend/.env -rw------- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 930 Nov 12 14:50 /home/ubuntu/projects/TechVina/backend/.env Step 4.6 – Configure RDS connection variables Open the editor:
nano ~/projects/TechVina/backend/.env Set these three variables using the current RDS endpoint and password:
DB_URL=jdbc:mysql://YOUR_RDS_ENDPOINT:3306/phone_store?sslMode=REQUIRED DB_USERNAME=admin DB_PASSWORD=YOUR_RDS_PASSWORD Replace YOUR_RDS_ENDPOINT and YOUR_RDS_PASSWORD with the actual RDS values. Leave Cognito variables at their template values for now. In Nano, press Ctrl+O, Enter, then Ctrl+X.
Verify only non-secret variables:
grep -E '^(DB_URL|DB_USERNAME)=' ~/projects/TechVina/backend/.env DB_URL=jdbc:mysql://YOUR_RDS_ENDPOINT:3306/phone_store?sslMode=REQUIRED DB_USERNAME=admin Step 4.7 – Generate and verify the JWT Secret Generate 64 random bytes (128 hexadecimal characters) and update .env without printing the secret:
JWT_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 64)" && sed -i "s|^JWT_SECRET=.*|JWT_SECRET=${JWT_SECRET}|" ~/projects/TechVina/backend/.env && unset JWT_SECRET Verify the format without exposing the value:
grep -Eq '^JWT_SECRET=[0-9a-f]{128}$' ~/projects/TechVina/backend/.env && echo "JWT_SECRET: OK" || echo "JWT_SECRET: INVALID" JWT_SECRET: OK Result: EC2 is accessible through Session Manager; Java 21, Maven 3.8.7, Git, MySQL Client, and AWS CLI work. The phone_store database contains 36 tables and 24 products. The Backend has been packaged as a 63 MB JAR; .env contains the RDS connection and JWT Secret. Cognito variables still contain their template values.

title: Create an S3 Interface endpoint
content:
Step 1 – Check the SQL file on GitHub Open GitHub and go to the TechVina repository in your own GitHub account. Select the master branch. On the Code tab, open database → full. Select phone_store.sql to view the SQL file directly in GitHub. Press Ctrl + F and search for CREATE DATABASE. Confirm that the statement contains the database name phone_store. Then find USE phone_store; to verify that the file selects the same database. These statements are already in the SQL file; do not execute them at this step. Search for CREATE TABLE and confirm that the file defines tables such as sanpham, danhmuc, phienban, anh and refreshtoken. Expected result: database/full/phone_store.sql exists in the repository and contains the schema and sample data for the phone_store database.
Step 2 – Retrieve Amazon RDS connection details In the AWS Console, select Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1. Open Aurora and RDS → Databases and select the techvina-mysql DB instance created in Section 5.4.1. Confirm that the Status is Available. Do not proceed with connection steps until the instance is available. Open Connectivity & security and locate Endpoint & port. Copy the Endpoint and note the Port (normally 3306). The endpoint is the RDS server hostname; it is not the phone_store database name. Open Configuration and check the Master username. Use the master password set when you created the RDS instance; it is not displayed again as plain text on the DB instance details page. In Connectivity & security, verify that VPC is techvina-vpc, Publicly accessible is No, and the attached VPC security group includes techvina-rds-sg. Use the following values for the subsequent MySQL connection:
Setting Value RDS endpoint Copy from Endpoint & port Port 3306 Master username admin (if you followed Section 5.4.1, Step 2) Master password Password configured for RDS Database name phone_store Expected result: RDS is Available, and the endpoint, port, username, and database name have been identified.
You will import phone_store.sql from EC2 in the same VPC in Section 5.5.1 – Step 3, after launching EC2 and connecting through Session Manager.

title: Prerequiste
content:
Step 1 – Prepare the AWS account Sign in to the AWS Management Console with a lab account allowed to create IAM, VPC, EC2, RDS, S3, CloudFront, Cognito, CloudWatch, and Systems Manager resources. Open Billing and Cost Management → Credits to review credit balance and expiration. Create an email spending alert in AWS Budgets → Create budget. Select Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1 in the Region selector. Use this Region for regional resources; CloudFront is global. Verify the AWS Account ID and service permissions in Singapore before provisioning resources. Step 2 – Prepare the GitHub repository Sign in to GitHub and open the TechVina source repository. Select Fork → Create fork to create a repository under your GitHub account. The fork URL follows https://github.com/<GITHUB_OWNER>/TechVina. Open your repository and verify the master branch along with .github/workflows/, .github/scripts/, .github/tests/, backend/, frontend/, and database/. Use the repository owned by your account when configuring GitHub Actions and GitHub OIDC in section 5.8. Step 3 – Install Git for Windows Open the Git for Windows download page, download the appropriate Windows installer, and run it. Complete the installation with Git Bash enabled. Git Bash provides a shell for Git commands and Bash scripts on Windows. Open Git Bash from the Start Menu and verify Git: git --version The terminal should display the installed Git version. The CI/CD steps use Git Bash to run git add, git commit, git push, and the Backend rollback test script.
Step 4 – Install Visual Studio Code Visit Visual Studio Code and install the Windows version. Open Visual Studio Code and choose Terminal → New Terminal. Use the arrow beside the Terminal + button to choose Git Bash as your shell. If it is unavailable, verify that Git for Windows was installed correctly. Visual Studio Code is used to edit .github/workflows/*.yml, .github/scripts/*.sh, and project source files before committing changes to GitHub.
Step 5 – Clone TechVina onto Windows In Git Bash, navigate to the parent folder where the project should be stored. To create the project in C:, for example, run: cd /c git clone https://github.com/<GITHUB_OWNER>/TechVina.git cd TechVina git branch --show-current git status --short Replace <GITHUB_OWNER> with the account that owns your deployment repository. git branch --show-current should return master for the repository’s master branch. git status --short should produce no lines for a clean working tree. In Visual Studio Code, choose File → Open Folder and open the cloned project (for example, C:\TechVina). Verify that frontend/, backend/, and .github/ appear in Explorer. When editing workflows in section 5.8, run Git commands and the Backend rollback test from Git Bash at the repository root. Do not run Bash scripts directly in Windows PowerShell unless bash is available in PATH.
Step 6 – Prepare the AWS working environment This workshop uses AWS Management Console, AWS CloudShell, EC2 Session Manager, Visual Studio Code, Git Bash, and GitHub Actions:
AWS Management Console: provision and configure AWS resources. AWS CloudShell: verify the AWS account and run AWS CLI commands in the browser. title: Proposal
content:
Building a Mobile Phone E-commerce Web Application on AWS Cloud 1. Executive Summary This project aims to build and deploy a mobile phone e-commerce web application on AWS for two main user groups: customers and administrators. Customers can browse products, search for phones, register, sign in, and place orders. Administrators can manage products, images, orders, and users within the application’s scope.
The application uses ReactJS for its user interface, Java Spring Boot for business logic, and MySQL for data storage. On AWS, Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudFront deliver the frontend and product images; Amazon EC2 runs the application server; Amazon RDS manages the database; Amazon Cognito authenticates users; and Amazon CloudWatch monitors operations. Amazon VPC and AWS IAM provide network isolation and access control.
The goal is to deliver an online, testable phone-store application while gaining practical experience deploying a multi-component web system on AWS.
2. Problem Statement Current challenges
A phone e-commerce application needs centralized management of products, accounts, and orders. When the application runs only on local computers, it is difficult to test Internet access, connections among components, and system operations in a realistic deployment environment.
Proposed solution
The team will build a system consisting of a user interface, an application server, and a database. ReactJS provides customer and administrator interfaces; Spring Boot exposes APIs and processes business operations; and MySQL stores application data. These components will be deployed on AWS and connected through appropriate networking and access permissions.
Amazon Cognito will support user registration, sign-in, and authentication. Amazon CloudWatch will be used to observe server health and application logs.
3. Solution Architecture The architecture comprises the following primary components: users access the application through Amazon CloudFront; the ReactJS frontend and product images are stored in Amazon S3; business requests are routed to the Spring Boot application running on Amazon EC2; and the application connects to a MySQL database hosted on Amazon RDS. Amazon Cognito provides user authentication, while Amazon CloudWatch provides monitoring.
AWS services used
Service Purpose Amazon VPC Provides the network environment for the application server and database. AWS IAM Manages access permissions to AWS resources. Amazon EC2 Hosts Java Spring Boot and its APIs. Amazon RDS Hosts and manages the MySQL database. Amazon S3 Stores the built ReactJS frontend and product images. Amazon CloudFront Delivers the frontend and images and routes requests to the application server. Amazon Cognito Supports registration, sign-in, and JWT-based authentication. Amazon CloudWatch Collects metrics and logs for system monitoring. Component design
Frontend: Customer and administrator interfaces use ReactJS, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Bootstrap. The production build is stored in S3 and delivered through CloudFront. Application server: Spring Boot runs on one EC2 instance in a public subnet, receiving business requests through CloudFront using the /api/* path. Database: RDS MySQL is deployed in private subnets, with database access allowed only from the application server. A Single-AZ database instance is selected for the workshop environment. Product images: Images are stored in S3 and delivered by CloudFront. The application server receives appropriate permissions to manage files. Authentication and monitoring: Cognito issues authentication tokens, which Spring Boot validates for protected requests. CloudWatch tracks EC2 metrics and application logs. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation phases
Analyze the phone-store requirements and define customer functions, administrator functions, and data flows. Design ReactJS interfaces, the MySQL data model, and Spring Boot APIs. Configure the AWS environment, including IAM, VPC, security groups, EC2, RDS, S3, CloudFront, Cognito, and CloudWatch. Deploy the frontend to S3 and CloudFront, deploy Spring Boot to EC2, connect RDS, and integrate Cognito. Test website access, authentication, product management, order placement, database connectivity, and system logs. Team responsibilities
Team member Responsibilities Mai Văn Tường UI design; customer and administrator ReactJS interfaces; API integration; system analysis and design. Hoàng Thanh Tài IAM, VPC, EC2, RDS, S3, and CloudFront configuration; AWS deployment; CloudWatch monitoring. Kiều Minh Quang Database design, MySQL management, data preparation, and API testing with Postman. Đỗ Mạnh Long Spring Boot development, JPA, Repository, Service, Controller, and REST APIs. Dương Quang Huy Amazon Cognito integration, registration, sign-in, JWT validation, and authorization. 5. Roadmap and Milestones Milestone 1 – Analysis and design: Complete functional requirements, UI designs, the database diagram, and the AWS architecture. Milestone 2 – Application development: Complete ReactJS interfaces, Spring Boot features, the MySQL database, and authentication integration. Milestone 3 – AWS infrastructure preparation: Configure networking, permissions, compute, database, and storage resources. Milestone 4 – Deployment and integration: Deploy the frontend, backend, and database to AWS and connect all components. Milestone 5 – Testing and completion: Test functions, authentication, and database connectivity; review logs and metrics; finalize workshop documentation. 6. Budget Estimation Estimated AWS infrastructure cost for one month
Service / Resource Cost (USD/month) Amazon EC2 and EBS storage 21.19 Amazon RDS MySQL and database storage 21.01 Amazon S3 0.18 Amazon CloudFront 0.00 Amazon Cognito 0.00 Amazon CloudWatch 0.00 Public IPv4 address 3.65 AWS IAM and Amazon VPC 0.00 Total estimated cost 46.03 USD/month 7. Risk Assessment Risk matrix
Risk Impact Likelihood Incorrect networking or access permissions prevent components from connecting High Medium Application server or database interruption during testing Medium Medium Authentication or authorization configuration errors High Medium Actual costs exceed estimates or available credits are insufficient Medium Medium Mitigation strategies
Validate network rules and permissions step by step; permit database connections only from the application server. Test functions and component connectivity after each deployment phase; inspect logs and metrics in CloudWatch. Validate JWTs and enforce appropriate customer and administrator permissions. Track costs in AWS Billing and remove resources that are no longer needed. Contingency plan
If a service fails, inspect the logs and configuration, then restart the relevant component when appropriate. Maintain source code and essential database backups to restore the workshop environment. 8. Expected Outcomes A working mobile phone e-commerce web application with customer and administrator interfaces. Successful deployment of ReactJS on S3 and CloudFront, Spring Boot on EC2, and MySQL on RDS. Cognito-based registration, sign-in, authentication, and authorization. Verified workflows for browsing products, managing products, placing orders, and persisting data. Visibility into application logs and server health through CloudWatch. Completed workshop documentation including an architecture diagram, deployment steps, testing screenshots, and resource clean-up instructions.

title: Test the Gateway Endpoint
content:
Step 1 – Create Security Groups In AWS Console, select Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1, then open VPC → Security groups → Create security group. Create the two security groups below in order.
Step 1.1 – Create the EC2 Backend Security Group Under Basic details, enter:
Console field Value Security group name techvina-ec2-sg Description Security group for TechVina Backend EC2 VPC Select techvina-vpc (10.20.0.0/16), not the Default VPC techvina-vpc is the VPC name, not the security group name. A security group name cannot be changed after creation.
Under Inbound rules, add two rules for HTTPS on Nginx and Let’s Encrypt:
Type Port Source Description HTTP 80 0.0.0.0/0 LetsEncrypt-HTTP HTTPS 443 AWS-managed prefix list com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing Allow-CloudFront-HTTPS Set Source type = Custom, search for cloudfront.origin-facing, and select the AWS-managed prefix list (for example pl-31a34658 in Singapore). Do not copy a prefix list ID from another Region. Do not expose TCP 8080 publicly. Nginx will proxy HTTPS traffic on port 443 to Spring Boot at 127.0.0.1:8080.
Port 80 is used for HTTP-01 certificate issuance/renewal and HTTP-to-HTTPS redirects. Port 443 accepts HTTPS origin traffic only from CloudFront. 5.7.1 configures DuckDNS, Nginx, and the certificate after EC2 is launched.
Security Group Description values must contain only accepted characters; LetsEncrypt-HTTP and Allow-CloudFront-HTTPS are valid descriptions.
Under Outbound rules, leave the AWS default rule unchanged:
Type Destination All traffic 0.0.0.0/0 Click Create security group. On its details page, confirm the name techvina-ec2-sg, VPC techvina-vpc, and the inbound TCP 80 rule from 0.0.0.0/0 and TCP 443 from the CloudFront prefix list. Do not add an inbound SSH 22 rule; this lab uses AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to access EC2.
Step 1.2 – Create the Amazon RDS MySQL Security Group Return to VPC → Security groups → Create security group. Under Basic details, enter:
Field Value Security group name techvina-rds-sg Description Security group for TechVina RDS MySQL VPC techvina-vpc Under Inbound rules, choose Add rule:
Field Value Type MYSQL/Aurora (automatically sets Port 3306), or Custom TCP with Port 3306 Source type Custom Source Search for techvina-ec2-sg and select its Security Group ID (sg-...) within techvina-vpc Description – optional MySQL access from TechVina EC2 Do not choose Anywhere-IPv4 or 0.0.0.0/0 for MySQL. The source must be the EC2 security group, not your computer’s IP address.
Leave Outbound rules at All traffic → 0.0.0.0/0, then click Create security group.
Step 1.3 – Verify Security Groups In VPC → Security groups, confirm that both security groups belong to techvina-vpc:
Security Group Inbound rule Outbound rule techvina-ec2-sg TCP 80 from 0.0.0.0/0; TCP 443 from the CloudFront origin-facing prefix list All traffic techvina-rds-sg TCP 3306 from techvina-ec2-sg All traffic Step 2 – Create the EC2 IAM Role Step 2.1 – Create the Role and attach SSM and CloudWatch permissions Open IAM → Roles → Create role. Under Trusted entity type, choose AWS service. Choose EC2 for Service or use case and Use case, then select Next. Under Add permissions, find and select both AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore and CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy. Select Next. Set Role name to techvina-ec2-ssm-role. Verify that both managed policies are selected, then choose Create role. Policy Purpose AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore Allows EC2 to use AWS Systems Manager, Session Manager, and receive SSM commands CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy Allows the CloudWatch Agent to send EC2 logs and metrics to CloudWatch Step 2.2 – Add read-only access to the Backend Artifacts S3 bucket Open IAM → Roles → techvina-ec2-ssm-role. On the Permissions tab, choose Add permissions → Create inline policy, then open the JSON editor. Paste the following policy. Replace <AWS_ACCOUNT_ID> with the AWS account ID of the lab account. Find it in the AWS Console account menu or run aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text in CloudShell: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "ReadTechVinaBackendReleases", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::techvina-backend-artifacts-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>/releases/*" } ] } Select Next, enter the policy name techvina-ec2-backend-s3-read-policy, and choose Create policy. The ARN references the techvina-backend-artifacts-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID> bucket created in 5.6.1. An IAM policy can be created before its referenced bucket exists. The bucket name in 5.6.1 must match this ARN exactly. If the bucket name changes because of a naming conflict, update the IAM policy ARN accordingly. The s3:GetObject permission is restricted to release objects under releases/.
Step 2.3 – Grant manual frontend S3 upload permissions to EC2 Under IAM → Roles → techvina-ec2-ssm-role → Permissions → Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON, grant s3:ListBucket and s3:PutObject for the frontend bucket. These permissions are required to build on EC2 and upload dist/ in 5.7.3.
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "ListFrontendBucket", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:ListBucket", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::techvina-frontend-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>" }, { "Sid": "UploadFrontendObjects", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:PutObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::techvina-frontend-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>/*" } ] } Replace <AWS_ACCOUNT_ID> and name the policy techvina-frontend-s3-upload. Choose Create policy. This policy deliberately does not include s3:DeleteObject, because the manual sync in 5.7.3 does not use --delete.
Step 2.4 – Verify the IAM Role Open IAM → Roles → techvina-ec2-ssm-role → Permissions and verify:
Policy type Policy name AWS managed AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore AWS managed CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy Inline techvina-ec2-backend-s3-read-policy Inline techvina-frontend-s3-upload Step 3 – Validate Both Security Groups must belong to the correct VPC. Do not allow public MySQL access. Confirm that techvina-ec2-ssm-role has both managed policies and both inline policies listed in Step 2.4.
